big_idea: Addition combines two parts into a total. We can swap the parts and the total stays the same.
learning_intention: We are learning to add two parts to find a total, recall addition facts up to 10, and notice that swapping the parts does not change the total.
student_learning_goal: I can recall addition facts up to 10 and show that 3+4 and 4+3 have the same total.
success_criteria: I can find the total when I put two groups together.
I can write an addition equation: part + part = total.
I can show that 3+4 and 4+3 have the same total using counters or a ten-frame.
lesson_specific_materials: The Adding Machine anchor poster posted on the front wall

OPTIONAL: Plus the Pup paper-bag (teacher copy) — if available; otherwise teacher voices both characters in two distinct voices, or substitutes two stuffed animals / paper-bag puppets / pictures on the anchor poster. Activity is unaffected.
Fact-triangle deck (30 cards) for the closing round
Lesson 1 fact-recall snapshot tracker — provided in assessment_suite stage

minds_on.activity_name: Plus the Pup and the Adding Machine
minds_on.hook: Plus has two paws full of treats. How many treats does Plus have ALTOGETHER?
minds_on.teacher_script:
Bring children to the carpet. Put on Plus the Pup the puppet. Have two small piles of treats (or paper treats) on the floor in front of him.

'Friends — meet Plus the Adding Pup. Plus loves to COMBINE things. Watch.' Hold up Plus's left paw with 4 treats. 'Plus has 4 treats here.' Hold up the right paw with 3 treats. 'And 3 treats here.' Wiggle Plus excitedly. 'Plus wants to know — how many treats ALTOGETHER?'

Take responses. Most children will say 7 immediately. Affirm. 'Yes — 7. When Plus puts his two paws together, he has 7 treats. That's what ADDITION does. We take two parts and put them together to find the TOTAL. We call those parts ADDENDS, and the total is called the SUM.' Write 4 + 3 = 7 on the board. Label: addend + addend = sum.

Now flip the puppet's paws so the 3 is on the left and the 4 is on the right. 'Hmm — Plus dropped his treats and picked them back up. Now there are 3 in this paw and 4 in that paw. Did the total CHANGE?' Wait. Some children will say yes (because the visual changed); most will say no. Push: 'Let's check.' Count together: 3 + 4 = 7. 'The total is still 7! It does NOT matter which addend comes first. 3 + 4 = 4 + 3.' Write the equation. Star it on the chart.

'Today we are going to PRACTISE adding facts up to 10, and we are going to PROVE that swapping the parts does not change the total. Plus the Pup is going to be in our classroom all week, and he will help us learn his Adding Machine.'
student_actions: Listen and watch as Plus the Pup demonstrates combining two paws of treats.
Predict whether the total changes when the paws swap. Verify by recounting.

steps.instruction: Whole group on the carpet: model 5 + 2 on the double ten-frame. Place 5 red counters in the top frame, 2 yellow counters in the top frame. Together count: 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7. Sum is 7. Then swap: 2 red and 5 yellow. Same sum, 7. Move to 4 + 3 the same way.
steps.teacher_prompt: Say to students: 'Watch the ten-frame. I'm going to put 5 RED counters in.' Place them. 'Now 2 YELLOW.' Place them. 'How many ALTOGETHER?' Count chorally. 'Now I'm going to take them all out and put 2 red and 5 yellow.' Show. 'How many altogether?' Same answer. 'See — 5+2 and 2+5 both give 7. The order does not matter.'

steps.instruction: Introduce the fact-family triangle. Hold up a triangle card with 4 at the top, 3 and 7 at the bottom. 'This triangle holds the facts 4+3=7 and 3+4=7. Plus is showing us that one triangle = two addition facts.' Children chant the two facts together, three triangles in a row.
steps.teacher_prompt: Say to students: 'Look at this triangle. The big number at the top is the SUM. The two small numbers at the bottom are the ADDENDS. So this triangle shows us 4+3=7 AND 3+4=7. Two facts, one triangle.' Show 3 triangles total: (4,3,7), (5,2,7), (6,4,10).

steps.instruction: Send pairs to three stations (~7 minutes each). Station A: Ten-Frame Adding Machine — partner draws two number cards 0-5, builds the sum on the double ten-frame, writes the equation. Station B: Triangle Two-for-One — partner draws fact triangles, both partners read the two facts aloud. Station C: Plus's Treat Toss — pairs roll two dice (1-5 each), make Plus's two paws, write the sum, then write the swapped fact.
steps.teacher_prompt: Say to students: 'You'll go to three stations with your partner. Each one practises a different part of the Adding Machine. Listen for the chime to switch.' 7-min rotations × 3.

steps.instruction: Circulate to record formative evidence on the fact-recall snapshot. Watch for: (a) fluent recall (within 3 sec), (b) developing recall (within 10 sec, sometimes finger counting), (c) emerging recall (always finger or counter counting).
steps.teacher_prompt: Stop at each pair. Hand them a flash card with one fact ≤10 (e.g., 6+2). Time silently. Mark fluent / developing / emerging on the tracker.

differentiation.for_emerging: Children whose recall is consistently emerging stay at Station A (Ten-Frame Adding Machine) for both rotations. Use only addend pairs that sum to 5 or less (e.g., 2+3, 1+4) until those are fluent. Skip the swapping step — focus on building the sum.
differentiation.for_extending: Stretch cards: addends that sum to 10 (e.g., 7+3, 6+4, 8+2). Bonus question: 'If 6+4=10, what other facts does this triangle hold?' (Answer: 4+6=10, 10-4=6, 10-6=4 — gentle preview of subtraction in Lesson 3.)
differentiation.for_ell_or_iep: Provide a sentence frame: '___ + ___ = ___'. Provide picture-supported addend cards (e.g., a card with 4 dots and the numeral 4). Pair with a strong-recall peer for Station C.
differentiation.for_movement_learners: Let the movement learner be the 'Adding Machine' — stand at the front, put one hand out (4 fingers), put the other hand out (3 fingers), have the class count the total. Body-on-fingers is the embodied form of addend + addend = sum.

formative_check.what_to_look_for: Three signals: (1) fluent recall of the +0, +1, +2 facts (most children); (2) recall of doubles (e.g., 5+5) and the 'easy 9s' (e.g., 1+9); (3) the 'awkward middle' facts (5+4, 6+3) that need extra practice. Tracking these three bands separates emerging, on-track, and exceeding learners.
formative_check.how_to_record: Tick the fact-recall snapshot tracker per child as you observe. The tracker has columns for fluent / developing / emerging plus a notes column for the 'awkward middle' facts.
tracker_columns: Recall developing or emerging for awkward middle (5+4, 6+3, 7+2)

discussion_prompts: Plus the Pup says 'I learned a new trick today!' What is Plus's trick?
If you know 6+4=10, what is the swapped fact?
Why does swapping the addends not change the sum?
Which fact felt the trickiest today? Which felt the easiest?
consolidation.exit_routine: Each child whispers to a partner: 'My favourite fact today was ___ + ___ = ___ AND its partner is ___ + ___ = ___.' Partners share a few examples with the class. Then each child returns their counters to their pair's bag and lines up at the door.

assessment_in_this_lesson.evidence_collected: Fact-recall snapshot covering facts to 10. Bands: fluent (≤3 sec), developing (≤10 sec), emerging (counts on fingers or counters). Plus a check on whether the child can produce the swapped fact for any given fact triangle.
assessment_in_this_lesson.rationale: Lesson 1 is the diagnostic gateway. Children whose recall is emerging on facts to 10 will struggle with Lesson 2 mental strategies (which require knowing facts to recall doubles and near-doubles). Children who can't yet produce the swapped fact will have difficulty with Lesson 3 fact families. Knowing both signals on day 1 lets the teacher plan Lesson 2 small groups proactively.

expanded_walkthrough.title: When the child counts on fingers for every fact even after the ten-frame demo — repairing fact recall vs. fact derivation in Grade 1
expanded_walkthrough.rationale:
The most common Grade-1 trap on B2.2 (recall facts to 10) is the child who can DERIVE every fact correctly but cannot RECALL any fact fluently. They count on fingers for 4+3 just as they did for 8+5. This is not a strategy failure — the strategies are working. It is a recall gap: the facts have not yet moved from 'work it out' to 'just know it'. The Lesson 1 fact-recall snapshot is designed to surface this. The script below covers what a teacher should DO when they observe a child finger-counting every fact — including the +0 and +1 facts that should be reflexive by Grade 1.

The distinction matters because Lesson 2's mental strategies (doubles, near-doubles, make-ten) ALL assume that the child has fluent recall of the doubles facts (1+1, 2+2, …, 5+5) and the near-double launching points. If those facts are still being derived, the make-ten strategy in Lesson 2 will collapse — the child will count on fingers for 8+2=10, then count on fingers for 10+3, instead of recognising 8+2 as a known fact.
expanded_walkthrough.setup: Pair is at Station C (Plus's Treat Toss). One child rolls 4 and 3 on the dice. The teacher watches the child's hands. The child puts up 4 fingers on one hand, 3 on the other, and starts counting from 1: 'one, two, three, four, five, six, seven'. The teacher steps in.
expanded_walkthrough.teacher_script:
Crouch beside the child. 'Let's stop for a second. I'm going to ask you something — if I say FOUR, can you SHOW me four without counting?' The child lifts 4 fingers. 'Yes! You just KNEW four. You didn't count to 4 — you knew it. Four is a know-it number for you.' Pause. 'Now if I say SEVEN — can you show me seven without counting?' Most children will count up: 1, 2, 3… 7. Some will sub-itise (2 hands, one with 5 + 2). 'OK — seven took a moment. Seven is still a work-it-out number for you. That's normal.'

Now set up the recall move. 'Today I want to help you turn 4 + 3 into a know-it fact. Watch.' Take Plus the Pup's two paws. 'Four in this paw.' Show 4 counters. 'Three in this paw.' Show 3. 'Don't count from 1. Look at 4 and 3 together.' Pause. The child looks. 'How many?' If the child counts on, gently stop them: 'Don't count from 1. Just LOOK and let the answer pop.' Sometimes the answer comes — '7'. Affirm: 'YES! That's a know-it fact for you now. Say it three times: 4 plus 3 is 7. 4 plus 3 is 7. 4 plus 3 is 7.' Have them physically chant.

Now swap the paws. '3 in this paw, 4 in this paw.' Pause. 'How many?' If the child counts on, stop again. 'You just told me 4+3=7. Does swapping change the total?' The child remembers the morning's lesson: 'No.' 'So 3+4 is also…' '7'. 'Right — that's another know-it fact for you. Say it three times.' Chant 3+4=7 three times.

By the time the child has chanted both versions three times, they have rehearsed the fact 6 times in 30 seconds. That's a strong recall step. Tick 'recall fluent' on the tracker for THIS specific fact (4+3 and 3+4). Move on to the next pair.

If the child STILL counts from 1 even after the chant: the recall path is jammed by the count-from-1 habit. Repair by removing finger access: 'Sit on your hands.' Then ask 4+3. The child has to use the visual sub-itising path (look at 4 dots, look at 3 dots, see 7) instead of the finger path. This is harder but more durable. Plan a daily 5-minute fact-fluency warm-up across the week with this child explicitly named.

Long-term recovery: send home a parent note with a fact-flash card set (the doubles, plus-1, and plus-0 facts to 10 — 18 cards total). Five minutes of flash a day for two weeks moves most children from 'counts every fact' to 'fluent on the easy half'.
expected_student_responses: (Confused) Counts every fact from 1 on fingers, including 1+1 and 2+0. Recall is essentially zero. Most common at the start of Grade 1 for transition learners.
(Mid) Fluent on +0 and +1 facts, finger-counts everything else. Knows the doubles 1+1 and 2+2, hesitates on 3+3 and beyond. Typical for early-to-mid-October Grade 1.
(Strong) Fluent on all facts to 10 except the awkward middle (5+4, 6+3, 7+2). Knows doubles, near-doubles, and the easy 9s. Typical of children who had strong K math.

(Stretched) Fluent on all facts to 10 AND can volunteer the swapped fact instantly. Beginning to recognise that fact-family triangles encode two facts at once. Ready for Lesson 3's subtraction-from-fact-family work.
common_misconceptions: Addition has to start at the bigger number. (Child believes 4 + 3 must be done in that order with the 4 first. Repair: explicitly model 3+4 alongside 4+3, both with the SAME ten-frame sum showing — visual proof of commutativity.)

The plus sign means 'count more'. (Child treats 4+3 as 'start at 4 and count 3 more', a count-on strategy that works but is not yet fact recall. Repair: this is not wrong but is not B2.2 — explicitly distinguish 'count-on' from 'recall' and tell the child the goal is to RECALL.)

Two facts that look different (4+3 and 3+4) must have different answers. (Visual conservation issue. Repair: physically swap the two-colour counters in the ten-frame WITHOUT removing them — children see the SAME counters, just rearranged. The total is unchanged because nothing left or arrived.)
recovery_moves: Use the chant. 'Three plus four equals seven, three plus four equals seven, three plus four equals seven.' Saying a fact aloud three times moves it from working memory toward long-term storage faster than any silent read.
Remove finger access for known-easy facts. Once the child has recalled 4+3 with help, ask them to do 4+3 again with hands behind their back. Forces the visual sub-itising path.
Pair every new fact with its swap immediately. Don't introduce 4+3 alone — always introduce 4+3 = 3+4. Cuts recall load in half because the child stores one combined fact, not two.
Build a 'know-it list' on the wall. As children master facts, write them on a class chart. Visible progress motivates the children whose recall is still emerging.

worksheet_brief.purpose: Independent practice of B2.2 (facts to 10) with explicit attention to commutativity (B2.1). Captures diagnostic-level evidence for the unit.

parts_outline.task: Six fact-family triangles. The child fills in the missing number on each triangle, then writes the two addition facts the triangle holds.
Four ten-frame addition scenes. Each scene shows red and yellow counters in the double ten-frame. The child writes the equation, then writes the swapped equation underneath.
Plus the Pup with 6 treats in one paw and an unknown number in the other paw. The total is 9. How many are in the second paw? The child draws the answer and writes the equation.
